qs.q: A 28-year-old atopic male with allergic rhinitis and asthma presents with food impaction and dysphagia. Symptoms fail to improve on high-dose PPI. Endoscopic biopsies from the mid-oesophagus show dense eosinophilic infiltration superficially. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic immune response characterised by eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophageal mucosa, often associated with atopy. It typically presents with dysphagia and food impaction and does not respond well to PPIs.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The oesophagus is a muscular tube that conveys food from the pharynx to the stomach. Its anatomy determines patterns of disease, bleeding, and surgical risk.

sections.p: A 25‑30 cm long conduit lying behind the trachea, crossing the diaphragm at the oesophageal hiatus, and ending at the gastro‑oesophageal junction.
b: Upper GI bleed source if above ligament of Treitz

sections.p: Four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis (inner circular, outer longitudinal), adventitia. Upper third striated muscle, middle mixed, lower smooth muscle.
b: Peristalsis coordinated by central pattern generator in brainstem
Lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) tone prevents reflux

sections.p: Anteriorly: trachea, left main bronchus; posteriorly: thoracic aorta (upper), vertebral bodies (lower). In neck, lies within visceral (pretracheal) fascia with thyroid, parathyroids, larynx.
b: Aortic aneurysm can compress oesophagus → dysphagia
Mediastinal infections may track along adventitia

sections.p: Upper third: inferior thyroid arteries; middle third: bronchial and oesophageal branches of the aorta; lower third: left gastric and inferior phrenic arteries.
b: Ischemic injury rare but can follow aortic surgery

sections.p: Sensory afferents via vagus (A‑δ fibers) and sympathetic fibers; motor via vagus (parasympathetic) to upper two thirds and the myenteric plexus for lower smooth muscle.
b: Vagal injury → loss of peristalsis, reflux
Recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in tracheoesophageal groove

sections.p: Propels bolus by coordinated peristalsis; LES maintains high‑pressure zone to prevent gastric contents reflux.
b: Dysfunction leads to dysphagia or gastro‑oesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

sections.p: Common problems: reflux, Barrett oesophagus, oesophageal cancer, foreign body impaction, caustic injury, and upper GI bleed. In low‑resource settings, TB oesophagitis and schistosomal granulomas occur.
b: TB or HIV‑related ulceration → bleeding, fistula

t.b: Visualise mucosa, obtain biopsies; answers presence of ulcer, Barrett, tumour
Detect strictures, perforation when endoscopy unavailable
Assess extrinsic compression, mediastinal spread of cancer

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: layer composition, blood supply zones, causes of upper GI bleed, and the progression from reflux to Barrett to adenocarcinoma.
b: Upper GI bleed above ligament of Treitz = oesophageal source
Barrett metaplasia is reversible but increases adenocarcinoma risk
Injury to recurrent laryngeal nerve can cause hoarseness

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden inability to swallow liquids (complete obstruction)
Chest pain with signs of perforation (subcutaneous emphysema, sepsis)

faq.q: Why does reflux cause Barrett oesophagus?
faq.a: Chronic acid exposure triggers replacement of squamous epithelium by columnar cells, which are more resistant but predispose to cancer.

faq.q: What is the significance of the LES pressure zone?
faq.a: It prevents gastric acid reflux; low pressure leads to GERD, high pressure causes achalasia.

faq.q: How does a foreign body appear on imaging?
faq.a: Radiopaque objects are seen on X‑ray; radiolucent items may be outlined by a barium swallow.
